groups.high: GDPR Article 22 addresses decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produce legal effects or similarly significantly affect an individual. Automated rejection of a credit application or consequential employment screening can fall within that scope; not every recommendation or analytical score does. Meaningful human involvement must be capable of influencing the decision, rather than merely endorsing an algorithmic result. Article 22(2) provides three exceptions: necessity for entering into or performing a contract, authorization by Union or Member State law containing suitable safeguards, and the individual's explicit consent. Convenience alone does not establish contractual necessity, and a generic assertion of public interest is not the statutory law exception. For the contract and explicit-consent exceptions, Article 22(3) requires suitable safeguards including at least human intervention, an opportunity to express one's viewpoint, and a right to contest the decision. The authorizing-law exception requires its own suitable protective measures. Special-category data introduce an additional restriction under Article 22(4): the relevant Article 9 explicit-consent or substantial-public-interest condition and suitable safeguards must apply. Information rights under Articles 13, 14, and 15 can require meaningful information about the logic, significance, and envisaged consequences. Article 21 objections are a related but distinct right, not a substitute for Article 22's conditions. Identify the decision, its consequences, the extent of genuine human review, the claimed exception, and the available challenge procedure before concluding that an automated system is lawful or prohibited.
groups.mid: GDPR Article 22 protects you from certain decisions made only by an automated system. This includes profiling, where software uses personal data to assess you. The decision must have a legal effect or affect you in a similarly significant way. A credit refusal or an important job decision may qualify. Not every score or recommendation does. A human review must be real. A person must be able to change the result. They cannot just approve what the computer says. Article 22(2) has three exceptions. A decision may be necessary to enter or perform a contract. Union or Member State law may authorize it with suitable safeguards. Or you may give explicit consent. A convenient shortcut is not necessarily needed for a contract. Saying public interest alone does not establish the law exception. For the contract and consent exceptions, Article 22(3) requires safeguards. These include at least human intervention, a chance to give your view, and a chance to contest the decision. For the law exception, the law must provide suitable protection. Article 22(4) adds limits for special-category data. Health data is an example. The relevant Article 9 condition must be explicit consent or substantial public interest, with suitable safeguards. Articles 13, 14, and 15 can require meaningful information about the logic, importance, and likely effects. Article 21 gives a separate right to object. Ask what decision was made, how it affects you, who really reviews it, which exception applies, and how to challenge it.
groups.low: GDPR Article 22 limits some decisions made only by a computer system. It includes profiling. Profiling means using your data to assess things about you. The decision must change your legal position or affect you in a similarly big way. A credit refusal or a major job decision may count. Not every score or suggested item counts. A human review must be real. The person must be able to change the result. Just saying yes to the computer is not enough. Article 22(2) has three exceptions. The decision may be needed to enter or carry out a contract. Union or Member State law may allow it with suitable safeguards. Or you may give explicit consent, meaning a clear agreement. Being easier for a firm does not make a decision needed for a contract. Just saying public interest does not prove the law allows it. Article 22(3) requires safeguards for the contract and consent exceptions. These protect your rights. You must at least be able to get human intervention, give your view, and contest the decision. For the law exception, the law must set suitable safeguards. Article 22(4) adds limits for special-category data, such as health data. Check the relevant Article 9 basis. It must be explicit consent or substantial public interest. Safeguards are needed too. Articles 13, 14, and 15 can require meaningful facts. These concern the logic and likely effects. Article 21 gives a separate right to object. Ask what was decided, why it matters, who can review it, what exception applies, and how to challenge it.
groups.source_review: EDPB EU guidance checked against original GDPR instrument, not amended UK GDPR. Article 22 exceptions and safeguards distinguished.
groups.notes: Corrected incomplete exception list and conflation of objections with Article 22 rights.

groups.high: Dark patterns, also termed deceptive design patterns, are interface choices that manipulate or obstruct users' privacy decisions. Under the GDPR, a consent interface must be assessed against the definition of consent in Article 4(11), the conditions in Article 7, and relevant guidance in Recitals 32, 42, and 43. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous; a misleading interface cannot manufacture valid agreement merely by recording a click. Preselected consent boxes, silence, or inactivity do not constitute the required affirmative indication. Concealed purposes, confusing controls, repeated pressure, and an unnecessarily difficult withdrawal path may undermine the applicable consent requirements. Article 7(3) requires withdrawal to be as easy as giving consent, and withdrawal does not retroactively invalidate processing that was lawful before it. Article 7(4) requires particular attention where a contract or service is conditional on consent to processing unnecessary for its performance. It does not mean every refusal must leave every conceivable service unchanged regardless of circumstances. Nor does the label dark pattern automatically establish that every visual nudge violates the GDPR; the actual design, information, freedom of choice, and processing basis matter. Controllers must be able to demonstrate consent where they rely on it, and the fairness and transparency principles remain relevant. Users can inspect what purposes are requested, whether optional choices are genuinely optional, and how to refuse or withdraw. Record a misleading screen and raise the concern with the controller or relevant supervisory authority rather than treating a confusing button as valid permission for unlimited use.
groups.mid: Dark patterns are designs that steer or trick people into choices about their data. They are also called deceptive design patterns. Under the GDPR, clicking a button does not by itself prove valid consent. Article 4(11) says consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous. This means a real choice, clear purposes, enough information, and a clear sign of agreement. Article 7 adds rules. Recitals 32, 42, and 43 help explain them. A preselected consent box is not your active agreement. Silence or doing nothing is not consent either. Hidden purposes, confusing controls, repeated pressure, or a hard-to-find withdrawal route may break the rules. Article 7(3) says withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it. Withdrawal does not make earlier lawful use unlawful after the fact. Article 7(4) matters when a service or contract depends on consent to data use that it does not need. But the law does not promise every service stays unchanged after every refusal. The facts matter. Nor is every visual nudge automatically a GDPR breach. Look at the design, what you are told, whether you have a free choice, and the basis for using data. A controller relying on consent must be able to show it had consent. Fairness and clear information matter too. Check each purpose and whether optional choices really are optional. Find how to refuse or withdraw. Save a misleading screen and complain to the controller or relevant data authority if needed.
groups.low: Dark patterns are tricks in a screen's design. They steer you toward a choice about your data. Another name is deceptive design patterns. A click alone does not prove valid consent under the GDPR. Article 4(11) says consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous. You need a real choice. You need to know the purposes. You need enough facts. You must clearly show agreement. Article 7 adds rules. Recitals 32, 42, and 43 help explain them. A box already ticked for you is not your active yes. Silence is not consent. Doing nothing is not consent. Hidden purposes and confusing buttons can cause problems. So can repeated pressure or making it hard to stop. Article 7(3) says it must be as easy to withdraw consent as to give it. This does not make earlier lawful use unlawful. Article 7(4) matters if a service demands consent for data use it does not need to carry out the contract. But not every refusal must leave every service unchanged. The facts matter. Not every nudge is a GDPR breach either. Check what the screen does. Check what it tells you. Check if your choice is free and what basis allows the data use. A controller that relies on consent must be able to show it had consent. Fairness and clear facts still matter. Read each purpose. Check if optional choices really are optional. Find how to refuse or withdraw. Save a misleading screen. You can raise the problem with the controller or the relevant data authority.
groups.source_review: EDPB deceptive-design and consent guidance checked; statutory provisions anchored to original EU GDPR.
groups.notes: Removed claim that every nudge is unlawful and that refusal can never affect any service; retained affirmative consent and withdrawal protections.

groups.high: GDPR Article 20 provides a qualified right to data portability, not a universal entitlement to transfer every record or an obligation to provide a particular API. It applies to personal data concerning the individual that they provided to a controller when processing is automated and based on consent or a contract. In EDPB guidance, provided data can include observed activity, such as usage records, but not necessarily the controller's inferred profiles or derived analysis. The individual can receive covered data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and transmit it to another controller without hindrance. CSV, JSON, and XML illustrate possible formats; Article 20 does not prescribe those exact formats, OAuth 2.0, real-time synchronization, or a universal API architecture. A readable document is not automatically a suitable portable dataset: practical machine processing and the nature of the data matter. Direct controller-to-controller transmission is available where technically feasible; controllers need not make unrelated systems universally compatible. The right does not apply to processing necessary for a public-interest task or exercise of official authority vested in the controller, and its exercise must not adversely affect others' rights and freedoms. Portability is distinct from Article 15 access and does not automatically erase the source copy; Article 17 erasure has separate conditions. Identify the data, processing basis, automated nature, intended recipient, and feasible format. The point is meaningful reuse and user control, with the statutory scope and safeguards intact, rather than assuming that downloading or transferring data cancels lawful retention duties.
groups.mid: GDPR Article 20 gives a right to move some personal data to another service. It is not a right to move every record. The data must concern you and be data you provided. The processing must be automated and based on consent or a contract. EDPB guidance says provided data can include observed use, such as usage records. It does not necessarily include profiles or analysis the controller inferred. You can receive covered data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format. You can send it to another controller without hindrance. Machine-readable means software can work with it. CSV, JSON, and XML are possible formats. The law does not require those exact formats. It does not require OAuth 2.0, real-time syncing, or one universal API. An API lets systems exchange data. A document that people can read is not always a useful portable dataset. The format must fit the data and allow practical machine use. You can ask for direct transfer between controllers where technically feasible. This does not require all systems to become compatible. The right does not apply to processing needed for a public-interest task or official authority vested in the controller. It must not harm other people's rights and freedoms. Article 15 access is a different right. Moving data does not automatically delete the old copy; Article 17 has separate erasure rules. Check which data qualify, why they are processed, whether processing is automated, who should receive them, and which format works. A transfer does not cancel a lawful duty to keep records.
groups.low: GDPR Article 20 lets you move some personal data to another service. It does not cover every record. The data must be about you and be data you provided. The processing must be automated. It must be based on consent or a contract. EDPB guidance says provided data can include observed use, such as usage records. It does not necessarily cover a profile or analysis the controller worked out about you. You can get covered data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format. This means software can work with it. You can send it to another controller without hindrance. CSV, JSON, and XML are examples. The law does not demand those exact formats. It does not demand OAuth 2.0, real-time syncing, or one universal API. An API lets systems exchange data. A document you can read is not always a useful portable dataset. Software must be able to use the data in a suitable way. You can ask for a direct transfer to another controller where technically feasible. That means where the systems can do it. The rule does not make all systems compatible. It does not cover processing needed for a public-interest task or the controller's official authority. Other people's rights and freedoms must not be harmed. Article 15 access is a separate right. Moving data does not automatically erase the old copy. Article 17 has separate rules for erasure. Check which data qualify, the basis for using them, whether processing is automated, who should get them, and a format that works. Moving data does not cancel a lawful duty to keep records.
groups.source_review: EDPB portability guidance and original Article 20 checked; observed and inferred data distinguished.
groups.notes: Removed invented universal API, OAuth and real-time obligations; no automatic erasure after transfer.

groups.high: The GDPR distinguishes notification to a supervisory authority from communication to affected individuals. Under Article 33, a controller must notify the competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours after becoming aware of a personal data breach, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. The clock is not automatically the moment an unknown attack occurred. If notification exceeds 72 hours, reasons for delay must accompany it; information may be supplied in phases without undue further delay when necessary. A processor must notify its controller without undue delay after awareness. Article 34 requires communication to affected individuals without undue delay when the breach is likely to result in a high risk, not a universal 72-hour deadline for every hacked user. The communication must use clear, plain language and explain the breach, a contact point, likely consequences, and measures taken or proposed. Exceptions can apply where protective measures such as effective encryption render the data unintelligible to unauthorized persons, subsequent measures remove the likely high risk, or individual communication would require disproportionate effort and equivalent public communication is used. A breach can involve accidental loss, destruction, alteration, or unauthorized disclosure or access, not only malicious hacking. Controllers must document breaches, effects, and remedial action even when notification is not required. Assess risk, identify the correct recipient, contain the incident, preserve evidence, and communicate the required facts without assuming that every incident automatically attracts a maximum fine.
groups.mid: The GDPR has different breach rules for a data authority and for affected people. A breach can mean lost or destroyed data. It can mean changed or wrongly disclosed data. It can also mean unauthorized access. It is not only hacking. Under Article 33, the controller must tell the competent supervisory authority without undue delay. Where feasible, it must do so within 72 hours after it becomes aware of the breach. It need not notify if the breach is unlikely to risk people's rights and freedoms. The clock does not always start when an unknown attack happened. If notice is later than 72 hours, reasons for delay must be given. Missing information can be sent in phases without undue further delay where needed. A processor must tell its controller without undue delay after it becomes aware. Article 34 concerns affected people. They must be told without undue delay when a breach is likely to create a high risk. There is no universal rule to tell every user within 72 hours. Use clear, plain language. Explain the breach, a contact point, likely effects, and steps taken or planned. Exceptions can apply. Effective encryption may make data unreadable to unauthorized people. Later measures may remove the likely high risk. If personal notices take disproportionate effort, an equally effective public notice may be used. The conditions matter. Controllers must document breaches even when notice is not required. They must record effects and remedial action too. Assess risk, tell the right recipient, contain the incident, and preserve evidence. A breach does not automatically mean the maximum fine.
groups.low: A data breach is not just a hack. Data may be lost, destroyed, changed, shared wrongly, or accessed without permission. The GDPR has different rules for telling an authority and telling people. Article 33 covers the competent supervisory authority. The controller must tell it without undue delay. Where feasible, it must do this within 72 hours after it becomes aware of the breach. There is an exception if the breach is unlikely to risk people's rights and freedoms. The clock does not always start when an unknown attack took place. If notice is late, give reasons for the delay. Facts can be sent in phases where needed, without undue further delay. A processor must tell its controller without undue delay after it becomes aware. Article 34 covers affected people. Tell them without undue delay if the breach is likely to cause a high risk. There is no rule to tell every hacked user within 72 hours. Use clear, plain words. Explain what happened. Give a contact point. Explain the likely effects and steps taken or planned. Exceptions may apply. Good encryption may make the data unreadable to those not allowed to see it. Later steps may remove the likely high risk. If separate notices would take disproportionate effort, an equally effective public notice may be used. Each exception has conditions. Controllers must record breaches, effects, and steps to fix them even if notice is not required. Check the risk. Tell the right people. Contain the incident and keep evidence. A breach does not automatically lead to the maximum fine.
groups.source_review: EDPB breach guidance and GDPR Articles 33–34 checked. User prompt itself conflates deadlines; corrected at all levels.
groups.notes: Distinguished risk versus high-risk thresholds and authority versus individual communication; no automatic fine or all-hacks deadline.

groups.high: The claim that Bangladesh's Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025 imposed seven years' imprisonment for every disclosure of sensitive data is overbroad. In the official consolidated text, Section 37 addressed processing sensitive personal data contrary to Section 7 without explicit consent or another applicable legal basis. Its maximum punishment was seven years' imprisonment, a fine of BDT 2 million, or both; a maximum is not an automatic sentence. Section 41 separately addressed specified unauthorized disclosure by someone who obtained personal data through work, with a maximum of five years' imprisonment, BDT 1.5 million, or both. The applicable elements must be established rather than treating the provisions as interchangeable. Section 2(23) included genetic and biometric data, ethnic or community-related data, political or philosophical opinions, religious or similar beliefs, trade-union membership, health, sexual orientation, specified criminal matters, and instantaneous geolocation, with additional categories possible under rules. Financial or ordinary location data should not be indiscriminately described as automatically within every sensitive-data category. Consent is also not the only possible statutory basis for every relevant use; Section 7 and applicable exceptions require examination. Temporal scope matters: Section 1(3) deferred Sections 31–46 and Section 23 to a government-notified date after eighteen months, and the official page now records repeal by the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026. This is an explanation of the specified historical instrument, not an assertion that its penalties commenced immediately in 2025 or remain the current law. Check the conduct, legal basis, commencement, and operative legislation before applying a penalty.
groups.mid: The claim about seven years for every sensitive-data disclosure is too broad. The law named in the question is Bangladesh's Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025. It had separate offences. The official text includes amendments. Section 37 concerned processing sensitive personal data contrary to Section 7. Processing means using or handling data. It covered a lack of explicit consent or another applicable legal basis. A legal basis is a reason the law allows. The maximum was seven years in prison, a BDT 2 million fine, or both. A maximum is not an automatic sentence. Section 41 was a different rule. It concerned specified unauthorized disclosure. This means sharing data without permission. It applied to someone who got personal data through work. Its maximum was five years in prison, BDT 1.5 million, or both. The facts must fit the offence. These sections are not the same. Section 2(23) listed sensitive categories. They included genetic and biometric data. They included data on ethnicity or community. Political or philosophical views were included. So were religious or similar beliefs. Trade-union membership was included. Health was included. So was sexual orientation. Specified criminal matters were included. So was instantaneous geolocation. This means where a person is at each moment. Rules could add categories. Financial data is not always sensitive under every category. Nor is ordinary location data. Check Section 7 and relevant exceptions; not every use has consent as its only possible basis. The date matters too. Section 1(3) delayed Sections 31–46 and Section 23. The government had to set a start date by notice. This had to be after eighteen months. The official page now names the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026. It says that law repealed the ordinance. This means it replaced the old law. This explains the historical 2025 instrument. It does not say those penalties started at once or remain current law. Check what happened. Check the legal basis and start date. Check the law in force before applying a penalty.
groups.low: Not every disclosure of sensitive data meant seven years in prison. The law named here is Bangladesh's Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025. It had different offences. The official text includes later changes. It had a rule in Section 37. It concerned processing sensitive personal data contrary to Section 7. Processing means using or handling data. It covered a lack of explicit consent or another applicable legal basis. A legal basis is a reason the law allows. The maximum was seven years in prison, a fine of BDT 2 million, or both. That was a maximum, not an automatic sentence. Section 41 was a different rule. It concerned specified unauthorized disclosure. That means sharing data without permission. The person had got the data through work. Its maximum was five years in prison, BDT 1.5 million, or both. The facts must fit the offence. Section 2(23) listed sensitive data. It included genetic and biometric data. It included data on ethnicity or community. It included political or philosophical views. Religious or similar beliefs were included. So was trade-union membership. Health was included. So was sexual orientation. Specified criminal matters were included. So was instantaneous geolocation. This means where a person is at each moment. Rules could add categories. Do not assume all financial data or ordinary location data fit every sensitive category. Check Section 7 and the exceptions. Consent is not the only possible legal basis for every use. Check the date too. Section 1(3) delayed Sections 31–46 and Section 23. A government notice had to set a date after eighteen months. The official page now names the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026. It says this repealed the ordinance. That means it replaced the old law. This explains the historical 2025 instrument. It does not mean its penalties started at once or are still current. Check what happened, the legal basis, the start date, and the law in force.
groups.source_review: Official consolidated Bengali text checked for Sections 1(3), 2(23), 37 and 41, including delayed commencement and repeal notice; historical scope explicit.
groups.notes: Corrected wrong section, sentence certainty, blanket disclosure claim, category expansion and immediate/current enforceability assumption.

groups.high: Profiling is not categorically prohibited by the GDPR. Article 4(4) defines it as automated use of personal data to evaluate personal aspects, including work performance, economic situation, health, preferences, interests, reliability, behavior, location, or movements. Article 22 becomes relevant where a decision is based solely on automated processing, including profiling, and produces legal or similarly significant effects. A routine recommendation does not automatically meet that threshold. Human involvement must be meaningful, with authority and competence to influence the outcome; a nominal sign-off does not necessarily remove a decision from Article 22. Article 22(2) permits exceptions for contractual necessity, authorization by Union or Member State law with suitable safeguards, or explicit consent. Public interest alone is not a free-standing substitute for the authorizing-law condition. For the contract and consent exceptions, safeguards must include at least human intervention, an opportunity to express a viewpoint, and contesting the decision. Article 22(4) restricts special-category data to the relevant explicit-consent or substantial-public-interest conditions with suitable measures. Articles 13–15 provide relevant transparency and access protections, including meaningful information about decision logic and consequences where required. Article 21 is distinct: objections to legitimate-interest or public-task processing depend on the relevant conditions, whereas an objection to direct marketing requires that processing, including related profiling, to stop for that purpose. Other GDPR requirements still apply even if Article 22 is not triggered. Examine the purpose, data, consequences, genuine human role, legal basis, and challenge route rather than assuming that all profiles are banned or all consent makes profiling lawful.
groups.mid: The GDPR does not ban all profiling. Article 4(4) defines profiling. It means using personal data automatically to assess things about you. These include work performance and money matters. They include health, preferences, interests, and reliability. Behavior, location, and movements count too. Article 22 limits some decisions made solely by automated processing. This includes profiling. A decision must have legal or similarly significant effects. A routine recommendation does not automatically qualify. Human involvement must be meaningful. The person must be able and allowed to change the outcome. They cannot just sign off the result. Article 22(2) has three exceptions. The decision may be needed for a contract. Union or Member State law may allow it with suitable safeguards. Or you may give explicit consent. A general claim of public interest does not replace the need for an authorizing law. The contract and consent exceptions need safeguards. These include at least human intervention. You must be able to express your view. You must be able to contest the decision. Article 22(4) adds restrictions for special-category data. The relevant condition must apply. This must be explicit consent or substantial public interest. Suitable measures are needed too. Articles 13–15 can require meaningful information about the logic and effects. Article 21 gives separate objection rights. For legitimate-interest or public-task processing, the relevant conditions must be assessed. If you object to direct marketing, that processing must stop for that purpose, including related profiling. Other GDPR rules still apply when Article 22 does not. Check the purpose, data, and effects. Check the real human role and legal basis. Find out how to challenge the result. Do not assume all profiles are banned or that any consent makes them lawful.
groups.low: The GDPR does not ban every profile. Article 4(4) explains profiling. It means using personal data automatically to assess things about someone. These include work performance and money matters. Health is included. So are preferences and interests. Reliability and behavior count too. So do location and movements. Article 22 limits some decisions made only by an automated system. It includes profiling. The decision must have legal effects or affect you in a similarly big way. A routine suggested item does not always count. A human must do a real review. They must be able and allowed to change the result. Just signing it off may not be enough. Article 22(2) has three exceptions. The decision may be needed for a contract. Union or Member State law may allow it with suitable safeguards. Or you may give explicit consent. Just saying public interest does not replace the need for an authorizing law. The contract and consent exceptions need safeguards. You must at least be able to get human intervention. You must be able to give your view. You must be able to contest the decision. Article 22(4) adds limits for special-category data. The relevant condition must apply. This must be explicit consent or substantial public interest. Suitable safeguards are needed too. Articles 13–15 can require meaningful facts about the logic and effects. Article 21 is separate. There are conditions for legitimate-interest or public-task use. These matter if you object to that use. If you object to direct marketing, the firm must stop that use. This includes related profiling for that purpose. Other GDPR rules still apply even if Article 22 does not. Check the purpose, data, and effects. Check who really reviews it. Check the legal basis. Find how to challenge the result. Not all profiles are banned. Not all consent makes them lawful.
groups.source_review: EU GDPR profiling definition, Article 21 objections and Article 22 conditions checked against original instrument and EDPB guidance; not amended UK law.
groups.notes: Replaced blanket profiling prohibition and generic public-interest exception with conditional rights and safeguards.
